warningSigns.label: rush
warningSigns.explanation: Scammers rush you so you have no time to check the story or talk to someone you trust.

warningSigns.label: request to keep it secret
warningSigns.explanation: Being told to keep it secret is a warning sign. Real family wants you to check.

warningSigns.label: gift cards
warningSigns.explanation: Only scammers tell you to buy gift cards and give them the numbers on the back.

warningSigns.label: wire transfer
warningSigns.explanation: Scammers ask for wire transfers because the money is very hard to get back.

warningSigns.label: cryptocurrency
warningSigns.explanation: No real business or government agency will demand payment in cryptocurrency.

warningSigns.label: payment app
warningSigns.explanation: Money sent through a payment app to a stranger is very hard to get back.

warningSigns.label: cash pickup
warningSigns.explanation: Real officials and real family never send a courier to collect cash or gold.

warningSigns.label: emergency story
warningSigns.explanation: Scammers often say a loved one is in jail or in an accident, so you panic and pay.

warningSigns.label: family member asking for money
warningSigns.explanation: Scammers can copy a loved one's voice, so a familiar voice is not proof.

warningSigns.label: caller claiming to be from the government
warningSigns.explanation: Government agencies never call to ask for money or personal information.

warningSigns.label: threats
warningSigns.explanation: Threats of arrest or losing benefits are meant to scare you into paying fast.

warningSigns.label: request to move your money
warningSigns.explanation: No bank or agency will ever tell you to move your money to protect it.

warningSigns.label: computer problem call
warningSigns.explanation: Real tech companies do not call out of the blue about a virus or ask to get into your computer.

warningSigns.label: caller claiming to be from a company you know
warningSigns.explanation: Scammers pretend to be from companies like Amazon and fake the caller ID. Check your account on the company's own website or app.

warningSigns.label: fee to collect a prize
warningSigns.explanation: Real prizes are free. Paying a fee or taxes to collect one is a scam.

warningSigns.label: sweetheart you have not met
warningSigns.explanation: Never send money to someone you have not met in person.

warningSigns.label: request to stay on the phone
warningSigns.explanation: Scammers keep you on the line so you cannot check with anyone else.

patterns.name: Family emergency scam
patterns.description: A caller pretends to be a grandchild or other relative in trouble, or someone speaking for them, and asks for money right away.
advice: Hang up and call your family member on a number you know is theirs.
If you cannot reach them, check with another family member.
Ask for your family's secret word if you have one.

patterns.name: Government impersonation scam
patterns.description: A caller claims to be from Social Security, the IRS, Medicare, the police or a court and demands money or personal information.
advice: Hang up. Call the agency yourself using a number you look up.
Do not trust caller ID. It can be faked.

patterns.name: Fake bank or fraud department call
patterns.description: A caller says your account is at risk and tells you to move your money, withdraw cash or share a code to protect it.
advice: Hang up and call the number on the back of your card or on your statement.
Never share a verification code with a caller.

patterns.name: Fake company call about an order
patterns.description: A call or text claims to be from a company like Amazon about a suspicious purchase, then says your identity or money is at risk.
advice: Do not trust the number on your caller ID or what the caller tells you.
Check your account on the company's own website or app, not with a number they give you.
Talk about it with someone you trust.

patterns.name: Tech support scam
patterns.description: A pop up or caller says your computer has a virus and asks for remote access or payment to fix it.
advice: Do not call numbers from pop ups and do not let a caller into your computer.
If you are unsure, talk to someone you trust.

patterns.name: Cash or gold courier scam
patterns.description: After a fake tech support or government call, someone is sent to your home or a public place to collect cash or gold.
advice: Do not hand cash or gold to anyone who comes to collect it.
Do not give your home address to a caller you do not know.

patterns.name: Romance scam
patterns.description: Someone you met online builds trust, then asks for money for an emergency, travel or fees.
advice: Never send money or gifts to someone you have not met in person.
Talk it over with family or a friend you trust.

patterns.name: Prize, sweepstakes or lottery scam
patterns.description: A caller says you won a prize, then asks you to pay fees or taxes first, or for your bank details.
advice: Real prizes are free. Never pay to collect one.
Never give bank or card details to claim a prize.

patterns.name: Cryptocurrency payment demand
patterns.description: A caller tells you to buy cryptocurrency or use a coin ATM to pay or to protect your money.
advice: Anyone who demands payment in cryptocurrency is a scammer.
Do not use a coin ATM because a caller told you to.

steps: Call the company that sold the gift card right away.
Tell them it was a scam and ask for your money back.
Keep the card and the receipt.
Call the wire transfer company right away, for example Western Union or MoneyGram.
Tell them it was a scam and ask them to reverse the transfer.
Contact the company that issued the money order right away and ask them to stop payment.
If you mailed it, call the U.S. Postal Inspection Service at 877 876 2455.
Report the payment in the app right away.
Ask the app company to reverse the payment.
Contact the exchange or the coin ATM company right away and ask them to reverse it.
Call the U.S. Postal Inspection Service right away at 877 876 2455 and ask them to stop the package.
If you used FedEx or UPS, call them right away.
Do not hand over any more cash or gold.
Report it to the FBI at ic3.gov.
Call your bank or credit union right away.
Tell them it was a scam and ask them to reverse the transfer.
If you paid by card, call the number on the back of the card right away and ask for a refund.
Otherwise, call the company you used to pay right away and tell them it was a scam.

resources.name: ReportFraud.ftc.gov
resources.whenToUse: Report any scam to the Federal Trade Commission, whether or not you paid.

resources.name: ic3.gov
resources.whenToUse: File a complaint with the FBI. The FBI asks people 60 and over who were targeted by fraud to report here.

resources.name: National Elder Fraud Hotline
resources.whenToUse: Free help from a case manager for people 60 and over, including help filing a report.
resources.hours: Monday to Friday, 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Eastern
